stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the profile of Jackson Pollock in Life magazine, August 1949, which asked whether he was the greatest living painter in the United States. Pollock painted by splattering, pouring, and dripping paint onto large canvases laid on the floor. His work showed no recognizable people, places, or objects.

stem: Many Americans in the 1950s found abstract paintings puzzling. Which feature of the paintings best explains that reaction?

options.text: The paintings were too small to see clearly from a distance
options.misconception: Pollock painted on large canvases, so small size was not the problem.

options.text: The paintings copied photographs too closely to enjoy
options.misconception: The paintings showed no recognizable objects, so they did not copy photographs.

options.text: The paintings showed no people, places, or objects to recognize
The paintings used only black paint and white paint
options.misconception: Pollock's paintings used many colors, so a lack of color was not the problem.

rationales.A: Pollock painted on large canvases, so small size was not the problem.
rationales.B: The paintings showed no recognizable objects, so they did not copy photographs.
rationales.C: Viewers look for something they know in a picture, and Pollock's work gave them nothing to recognize.
rationales.D: Pollock's paintings used many colors, so a lack of color was not the problem.
rationales.general:
1. People read a painting by finding something they know in it, a face or a field.
2. Pollock's canvases show drips and pours, with no person, place, or object.
3. With nothing to recognize, viewers had no familiar way in, so the work puzzled them.
Remember: Art puzzles people most when it takes away the familiar thing they use to read it.
